title: Taking over the minstrel band and meeting the Verrett brothers in Homer, Louisiana
summary: White describes the minstrel orchestra, becoming bandmaster, and playing a winter in Homer with the Verrett brothers' seven-piece band.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: Was it like an orchestra or brass band? Out of that we had always a ten piece orchestra

to play the show in the pit. We had violinists, piccolo players, bass viol players, all of the instruments that go along. We had five clarinets in this band, and a fine piccolo player, Jared. And later on we got Clarence Owens, who now directs the 8th Regiment Band in Chicago. 8th Illinois Regiment. Ward officer Clarence Owens. The next season Jeff quit, and the manager of the of the Minstrel show asked me would I take the band over. I said, Charles E. Boeing. And I did. But I didn't complete the season, because another show offered me more money, and that was the Harveys Minstrel. Their home was in St. Paul, Minnesota, but they call it the New Orleans Minstrels. Never had seen New Orleans. The closest they ever got to New Orleans was when the winter season closed in Homer, Louisiana. And the two fine Pullman cars put up on the siding there. And while in Homer for a few days, I chanced to meet Arthur and Albert Verrett in 1917. Was Bunk Johnson around in that time? Bunk Johnson was around in those days. Bunk Johnson was definitely around. Well, I played a winter down there with the Verrett boys, Arthur and Albert Verrett. They had a seven piece orchestra down there. Albert played the violin and conducted the orchestra. And he was an excellent reader. That's Albert. But he was tripled. And Arthur played the saxophone and clarinet. I played trumpet. Young, Billy Young. I forgot what his father's name was. But anyhow, everybody called him Professor Young. He was not in Homer at that time, but Young was our trombone player. And Arthur and Albert had a sister who played the piano very well, but all halls did not have pianos in them. So we had a good bass player. And his name was Harrison. And we had a drummer. We called him Neegi. And that's all I ever knew from my whole state out there. He was a drummer, a very good drummer. And we had a banjo player. He was a barber down there. And if I'm not mistaken, I think his name was Barnes, I believe.

No, no. Banjo player. Banjo player. There were two Barnes's down there. But I think this fella's name was Barnes too. Isaac Barnes, I believe. That was in the Barnes that Louis went to. I believe. And during this winter down there while I was there, they advertised that this fella, another Barnes there who all tried to have a man around, he sent to New Orleans and brought Louis up there to play with him. I never got a chance to meet Louis personally, but I heard him the night of the affair. We had an engagement also. We used to play out both ends of the bar, up north end and up the south end. Always the Cajuns, wherever the Verrett boys were playing, where they flocked just like a bunch of blackbirds to a rice field. They were crowded. We were never without an audience of hundreds for any of our engagements. That's how good the Verrett brothers orchestra was at home. Well, I had begun to absorb a little bit of the New Orleans style of playing, because the fellas would tell me, listen to so-and-so, listen to so-and-so, listen to this fella, listen to that one and so forth. And the solid beat and the legato tone, the sort of a languid tone, you know. I had begun to develop a part of it from a fella named, one-armed fella named Joe Porter. Joe Porter.
